title: The sun visits his son
hook: the sun visits the son he grew apart from and is welcomed with black sesame; why Sankranti sweets come with sweet words
carry: sankranti mends bonds: sweet sesame, sweet words

segments.voice: Yesterday, Makar Sankranti and Bhishma on his bed of arrows, waiting for the sun to turn. Your line was uttarayana, the sun's bright half, when good things begin. Today, the same day, from the kitchen.

Surya, the sun, has a son named Shani, the slow, serious planet people worry about. Their story isn't a happy one. In many tellings, Surya kept his distance from the boy, Shani grew up hurt, and father and son hardly spoke. But the sun keeps moving, sign to sign, all year. And Makara, the sign the sun enters at Sankranti, belongs in Hindu astrology to Shani. It's his house. So once a year the father arrives at his son's door. And the son has to decide how to open it.
screen: `A FATHER AND A SON, APART.` → `MAKARA IS SHANI'S HOUSE.` → `THE SUN AT HIS SON'S DOOR.`

segments.voice: As many families tell it, Shani's house had almost nothing in it. All he could offer was black sesame. He gave it to his father anyway, and Surya was moved, and blessed him, and father and son made peace. It's a folk story, not from the old epics, but it's one of the reasons people give for why sesame is everywhere on this day. In Maharashtra, people go visiting with little sweets of sesame and jaggery, the dark unrefined sugar, called til-gul. You hand one to a neighbor, a cousin, a friend you've had words with, and say: til-gul ghya, god god bola. Take this sesame and jaggery, and speak sweetly. Sesame is small and sticks together; jaggery is sweet. Here's the teaching. Hindus treat speech as part of dharma, the right way to live. An old Sanskrit verse puts it plainly: speak what is true, and speak it kindly. And Sankranti, the first day of the bright half, is a day for mending bonds and for dana, a gift given freely. People bathe at dawn, in a river if they can, and give sesame, grain, blankets or food to someone in need. In Punjab, the night before is Lohri, with bonfires; in Assam, Bhogali Bihu, a feast. And today: a sesame sweet is a small way to say what's hard to say out loud. Sorry. Let's start again. If a father and a son who barely spoke could do it at a door, two friends can do it with a sweet.
screen: `SHANI OFFERS BLACK SESAME.` · `TIL-GUL GHYA, GOD GOD BOLA.` · `SPEAK WHAT IS TRUE, AND SPEAK IT KINDLY.` · `DANA: A GIFT GIVEN FREELY.` · then, large: `SWEET SESAME, SWEET WORDS.`

segments.voice: Think of one person you've had sharp words with this year, small or big. Picture pressing one sesame sweet into their palm, no speech, just: take this, and let's speak sweetly. Maybe their face softens, maybe it doesn't; that part isn't yours. If you pray, ask for kind speech this year, in your own words. Your part is the sweet and the words.
Makar Sankranti. The sun's crossing into Shani's sign, kept with sesame and sweet words, a dawn bath, and a gift given freely.
Your line: sankranti mends bonds: sweet sesame, sweet words. Tomorrow, a pot that's meant to boil over. See you then.
